title: Definition of Ready vs. Done: Safe to Start, Honest to Finish
summary: Ready says you know enough to start; Done says you've done enough to finish. What the Scrum Guide says about each, where they go wrong and how to keep both lists short.
author: Nguyen Le Phong
html:
Sprint planning, halfway through. Someone points at a ticket: "Is this one ready?" The PO says the goal is clear enough. The engineer says nobody knows yet what the payments API returns on a timeout. QA asks what "done" means for analytics and the empty-cart case. Nobody's arguing about vocabulary. They're arguing about two different moments: when it's safe to start, and when it's honest to say you've finished.

Definition of Ready and Definition of Done are the team's agreements for those two moments. Ready guards the start: is there enough shared understanding to begin without walking straight into avoidable confusion? Done guards the finish: does "finished" actually mean finished? Here's what each one is, where each goes wrong, and how to keep both short enough to be useful.

Only one of them is in the Scrum Guide

This surprises people. The Scrum Guide makes the Definition of Done a formal commitment: it's "a formal description of the state of the Increment when it meets the quality measures required for the product." It's strict about it, too. "If a Product Backlog item does not meet the Definition of Done, it cannot be released or even presented at the Sprint Review." The item goes back to the Product Backlog. And if the organization has a Definition of Done as a standard, every Scrum team has to follow it as a minimum.

Definition of Ready isn't in there at all. The closest the guide gets is one line about refinement: items "that can be Done by the Scrum Team within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in a Sprint Planning event." So Done is part of Scrum itself, and Ready is a practice many teams add on top. That difference matters later, when we get to how Ready goes wrong.

Ready: enough clarity to start

A useful Definition of Ready doesn't ask for certainty. If it did, nothing important would ever start. It asks for enough shared understanding: the user need is named, the outcome is clear, big dependencies are known, acceptance criteria can be tested and the work is small enough to finish in a sprint.

If you need a starting list, Bill Wake's INVEST checklist from 2003 still holds up: a good story is Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small and Testable (XP123). Most team Ready lists end up as some local version of those six words.

Ready also has to leave room for discovery. Some work is ready because the next learning step is clear, even though the answers aren't. A spike, a prototype or a technical investigation is ready when three things are written down: the question, the timebox and the decision the answer will unlock. "Spike: can the payments API give us idempotency keys? Two days. Decides whether we build our own dedupe table." That's ready.

Where Ready goes wrong

Mike Cohn warns that a strict Definition of Ready can get "dangerously close to stage-gate process", which in his view is basically waterfall (Mountain Goat Software). His example of a rule to avoid: "Each story must be accompanied by a detailed mock up of all new screens before we start work." Agile teams need design, build and test to overlap. A rule that forces one to finish before the next begins kills that overlap.

His fix is to write guidelines rather than rules. The mockup rule becomes: rough mockups have been started and are far enough along that the open questions can be settled during the sprint. He makes one exception for dependencies on other teams or vendors, where waiting for an answer before you start often really is the right call.

Done: the bar before work leaves the team

Definition of Done lives at the other end. It's the quality bar every item has to clear before it counts. A typical one for a web product team might read:

  • Code is reviewed and merged to main.
  • Tests are added or updated, and CI is green.
  • Basic accessibility is checked: keyboard, labels, contrast.
  • Analytics events are wired if the screen needs tracking.
  • Release notes or docs are updated for anything users will notice.
  • It's deployed to the environment the team agreed on, behind a flag if the rollout is risky.

Don't mix up Done with acceptance criteria. Acceptance criteria belong to one story and say what that story must do. The Definition of Done applies to every story and says how well anything has to be built before it ships. A story can meet all its acceptance criteria and still not be done because nobody wrote the tests.

Keep both lists short, and let real pain write them

A Ready list with twenty items gets ignored, or worse, gets used as a weapon ("not ready, bounced"). A Done list that tries to cover every concern turns into background noise. The good ones name the few things that keep hurting this team when they're missed. Acceptance criteria keep being vague? Put that in Ready. Analytics keeps getting forgotten? Put it in Done.

Both lists also take the personal bargaining out of delivery. Without them, the quality bar depends on who's reviewing, who's tired and how close the deadline feels. With them, there's a shared standard to point at. A developer asking for acceptance criteria isn't being difficult. QA asking how a case will be verified isn't being picky. Product asking for release notes isn't moving the goalposts, if the team already agreed that user-facing changes need them.

Neither list belongs to one role. Ready isn't only the PO's job and Done isn't only engineering's. Design, QA, data, support and security may each own a line, depending on the product. It works best when the whole team treats it as its own agreement. Once it becomes a form one person fills in for another, it stops working.

Change them when something breaks

A definition that never changes is probably being ignored. After an incident, a missed tracking event, a confusing release or a third sprint in a row with spillover, bring both lists to the retro and ask whether one line should change. Maybe dependency risk needs naming earlier. Maybe risky rollouts need a feature flag in Done. Maybe performance checks matter for one kind of work and not the rest.

A simple health check: Ready should mean fewer avoidable surprises after you start, and Done should mean less hidden debt after you finish. If either one mostly creates extra meetings, delays or blame, it has drifted away from its job.

Try this week

  • Write your current Definition of Done on one screen. If it doesn't fit, cut it to the lines that actually hurt when missed.
  • Reword one Ready rule as a guideline, Cohn style: "started and far enough along" instead of "finished."
  • For the next spike, write the question, the timebox and the decision it unlocks before anyone starts.
  • At the next retro, ask: which item this sprint met its acceptance criteria but wasn't really done?

Next time a ticket feels stuck between "almost ready" and "almost done", ask which promise is unclear. Do we know enough to start? Have we done enough to finish? Most delivery friction starts when two people use the same word and mean different things by it. For the bigger picture of how these fit into a sprint, see Agile and Scrum in practice.

faqs.q: What's the difference between Definition of Ready and Definition of Done?
faqs.a: Definition of Ready is the team's agreement on when a backlog item is clear enough to start. Definition of Done is the quality bar every item must meet before it counts as finished. Ready protects the start of work, Done protects the finish.

faqs.q: Is Definition of Ready part of Scrum?
faqs.a: No. The Scrum Guide makes the Definition of Done a formal commitment for the Increment but never mentions a Definition of Ready. The closest it gets is saying that items the team can finish within one Sprint are deemed ready for selection in Sprint Planning. Ready is a practice many teams add on top.

faqs.q: What should a Definition of Ready include?
faqs.a: A short set of guidelines: the user need and outcome are clear, big dependencies are known, acceptance criteria are testable and the item is small enough for one sprint. Bill Wake's INVEST checklist (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable) is a good starting point.

faqs.q: Can a Definition of Ready slow a team down?
faqs.a: Yes. Mike Cohn warns that strict Ready rules can drift toward a stage-gate process, for example requiring detailed mockups of every screen before work starts. He recommends guidelines instead, such as mockups that are started and far enough along to resolve the rest during the sprint.

faqs.q: How is Definition of Done different from acceptance criteria?
faqs.a: Acceptance criteria belong to a single story and describe what it must do. The Definition of Done applies to every story and describes the quality bar, such as review, tests, accessibility checks and deployment. A story can pass its acceptance criteria and still not be done.
